Pester

/PES-ter/ — rhymes with jester · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To pester someone is to bother them again and again with annoying requests, questions, or behavior.

The kids pestered their dad for ice cream until he finally gave in.

Worked Example

Maya's little brother keeps asking 'Are we there yet?' every five minutes during the long car ride, even though she's told him to stop.

The brother's behavior is relentless—he keeps doing the same annoying thing over and over. That repeated quality of the annoyance is what pester captures. 'Bother' could work, but pester is more precise because it specifically names the wearing-down effect of repetition.

How Pester Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

bother

bother: to disturb someone in a small way

bug

bug: to annoy someone in a casual, nagging way

nag

nag: to keep demanding or complaining at someone

Antonyms

appease

appease: to calm someone by granting their wishes

soothe

soothe: to gently calm and comfort someone

How Strong Is It? — annoy → bother → hound → pester

annoy vs. pester

annoy vs. pester: Annoy is weaker than pester: something can annoy you just once, while to pester is to come back with the same request again and again.

bother vs. pester

bother vs. pester: Bother is weaker than pester; a bother interrupts you now and then, but someone who pesters you keeps at it relentlessly until you give in.

hound vs. pester

hound vs. pester: Hound is stronger than pester: to pester is to nag someone repeatedly, while to hound is to pursue them so persistently they can never escape.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — empestrer

Root — empestrer: to hobble or entangle an animal (from a herdsman's hobbling rope) (Old French, from Vulgar Latin *impastoriare)

Put it together

Put it together: Pester began as 'to hobble or entangle,' like a rope tied around an animal's legs. Someone who pesters you keeps you tangled up — snagging your attention again and again — a sense later strengthened by the word's accidental resemblance to 'pest.'

Use the root in a new word: pasture

Use the root in a new word: pasture: The horses grazed all afternoon in the pasture — the same Latin pastor ('herdsman') root hides inside pester, which originally meant hobbling an animal with a herdsman's rope.

Root Check

Word Choice

informal / conversational

Use pester when someone's annoying behavior happens over and over — it's perfect for describing a kid who keeps asking for the same thing repeatedly. In formal writing, 'bother' or 'trouble' might be more appropriate, but pester captures the worn-down, accumulated annoyance that repetition creates.
